title: How does garbage collection work in Java (reachability, mark-and-sweep, generational heap, GC types), and what algorithms does the JVM use?
shortTitle: How does garbage collection work in Java, and what algorithms does the JVM use?

s1_definition.profdef: Garbage collection is the JVM's automatic memory management that reclaims heap objects no longer reachable from any live root. It determines liveness by reachability: starting from GC roots such as live stack variables, static fields, and active threads, it marks everything reachable and treats the rest as garbage. The classic algorithm is mark-and-sweep, often extended with compaction or copying. Because most objects die young, the heap is generational, with cheap frequent minor collections on the young area and rarer expensive collections on the old area. The JVM ships several collectors, including Serial, Parallel, CMS (now removed), G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah, each trading throughput against pause time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India periodically audits its storage vault to remove boxes nobody can reach anymore. The auditors start from the people and ledgers that are definitely active, the roots, and follow every chain of references to mark which boxes are still reachable. Any box that no active chain leads to is declared abandoned and removed, which is mark-and-sweep. Because most paperwork is thrown away quickly, the auditors sweep the busy intake area constantly and quickly, and only occasionally do a big, slow audit of the long-term archive. The bank can even choose different audit teams depending on whether it values speed of work or short interruptions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects by marking from roots and sweeping the rest, using a generational heap and a choice of collectors that trade throughput against pause time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Garbage collection is the JVM's automatic memory management that reclaims heap objects no longer reachable from any live root. It determines liveness by reachability: starting from GC roots such as live stack variables, static fields, and active threads, it marks everything reachable and treats the rest as garbage. The classic algorithm is mark-and-sweep, often extended with compaction or copying. Because most objects die young, the heap is generational, with cheap frequent minor collections on the young area and rarer expensive collections on the old area. The JVM ships several collectors, including Serial, Parallel, CMS (now removed), G1, ZGC, and Shenandoah, each trading throughput against pause time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India periodically audits its storage vault to remove boxes nobody can reach anymore. The auditors start from the people and ledgers that are definitely active, the roots, and follow every chain of references to mark which boxes are still reachable. Any box that no active chain leads to is declared abandoned and removed, which is mark-and-sweep. Because most paperwork is thrown away quickly, the auditors sweep the busy intake area constantly and quickly, and only occasionally do a big, slow audit of the long-term archive. The bank can even choose different audit teams depending on whether it values speed of work or short interruptions.

**One line to remember:** Garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects by marking from roots and sweeping the rest, using a generational heap and a choice of collectors that trade throughput against pause time.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is reachability, not reference counting. The collector starts from a set of GC roots, which include local variables on the stacks of live threads, static fields, JNI references, and active thread objects. It follows every reference from those roots, marking each object it can reach as live. Anything not marked is unreachable and therefore garbage. This approach correctly handles cycles, where two objects reference each other but neither is reachable from a root, which naive reference counting cannot collect.

The classic algorithm is mark-and-sweep. In the mark phase the collector traverses the object graph from the roots and marks live objects. In the sweep phase it walks the heap and reclaims everything unmarked. A problem with plain sweep is fragmentation, so many collectors add a compact phase that slides live objects together to leave one contiguous free block, or use copying, which moves survivors into a fresh space and abandons the old one wholesale. Copying is naturally fragmentation-free, which is why the young generation uses it.

The generational design builds on the weak generational hypothesis that most objects die young. New objects go into the young generation, which is collected by frequent, cheap minor collections. Survivors age and eventually get promoted to the old generation, which is collected by rarer, more expensive collections. People speak of minor collections on the young area and major or full collections involving the old area.

The JVM offers several collectors you select with flags. The Serial collector uses a single thread and suits small heaps. The Parallel collector uses many threads to maximize throughput and was long the default. The G1 collector, the modern default, divides the heap into many regions and aims to meet a pause-time goal by collecting the regions with the most garbage first, which is where the name Garbage-First comes from. For very large heaps with ultra-low pause requirements there are ZGC and Shenandoah, which do most of their work concurrently with the application. A senior nuance is that stop-the-world pauses happen because the collector must see a consistent object graph, so the choice of collector is really a choice about how much pause you can tolerate versus how much throughput you need; a batch job may prefer Parallel while a latency-sensitive trading service may prefer G1, ZGC, or Shenandoah.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's payment service created temporary objects for every request, and the team wanted to confirm that once those objects were no longer referenced, they were automatically reclaimed without any manual freeing. This is exactly reachability-based garbage collection, because once the last reference to a temporary object is dropped, no chain from a root reaches it, so it becomes eligible and the collector reclaims it.

Problem 2 — The team suspected a cyclic structure, where two objects referenced each other, might never be collected. This is exactly why reachability beats reference counting, because even a cycle with no root reaching it is correctly identified as garbage.

In the mini-project we demonstrate eligibility and cycles. We define an `Account`, a `TransactionBatch` that creates temporary objects and then drops their references, and a small cyclic pair of nodes to show cycles are collectible. The demo processes transactions for Rajesh and Priya, nulls out references, requests a collection hint, and logs reachability reasoning. We run with GC logging so the reader can see collections happen.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/gc/GcDemo.java

# Run with G1 (modern default) and GC logging
java -XX:+UseG1GC -Xlog:gc*:stdout:time,level,tags \
     -cp target/classes com.bank.gc.GcDemo

# Try other collectors:
#   -XX:+UseParallelGC   (throughput)
#   -XX:+UseZGC          (ultra-low pause, large heaps)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh (SAV2001, 1000000) and Priya (CUR3001, 250000), a transfer of 50000, and a cyclic pair of nodes A and B.

Step 1: The accounts are created on the heap and remain reachable from the main method's stack, so they are roots-reachable and will not be collected while main holds them.

Step 2: batch.process runs and creates a temporary receipt string local to the method. During the method, that string is reachable from the method's frame. The transfer mutates the heap accounts, leaving Rajesh at 950000 and Priya at 300000.

Step 3: When process returns, its stack frame is popped, so the receipt string is no longer referenced by anything. No chain from a root reaches it, so it is now eligible for garbage collection, even though the collector may not run immediately.

Step 4: Two Node objects A and B are created and linked to each other, forming a cycle. The local variables a and b are then set to null, removing the only roots. Even though A and B still reference each other, no root reaches either, so the reachability-based collector correctly marks both as garbage, which reference counting could not do.

Step 5: System.gc is called as a hint. The JVM may run a collection, during which it marks from the roots, finds the accounts still live, finds the receipt and the cycle unreachable, and reclaims them. The demo logs the reachability reasoning at each stage.

```text
[INFO] Processed RCPT-Rajesh-50000 → Rajesh now Rs.950000
[INFO] Temporary batch objects now unreachable → GC-eligible
[INFO] Cycle A<->B has no root → still GC-eligible (reachability wins)
[INFO] Requested GC hint; collection timing is JVM-decided
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  GC ROOTS: live stack vars, static fields, active threads
    │ mark reachable
    ▼
  rajesh ─▶ Account(SAV2001)   LIVE (reachable) → kept
  priya  ─▶ Account(CUR3001)   LIVE (reachable) → kept

  receipt (after process returns) ── no root ──▶ GARBAGE → swept
  A ⇄ B cycle (a=null,b=null)     ── no root ──▶ GARBAGE → swept

  Phases:  MARK (from roots) → SWEEP (reclaim unmarked)
           → optional COMPACT/COPY (defragment)
  Generational: minor GC (young, frequent/cheap) ; full GC (old, rare/costly)
  Collectors: Serial | Parallel | G1(default) | ZGC | Shenandoah
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — GC Strategy per Banking Workload ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Payment API (latency-sensitive)                   │
  │   → G1 / ZGC : small predictable pauses           │
  ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Nightly Statement Batch (throughput-sensitive)    │
  │   → Parallel GC : max throughput, pauses tolerable │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  GC logs → Prometheus → Grafana (pause P99, allocation rate)
  Alert if full GC frequency or pause time crosses threshold.
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — GC algorithm & collector choice ═══

  ── Reachability vs reference counting ──
  reachability: mark from roots, sweep rest → handles cycles ✓
  ref counting: cycle keeps count > 0 → leaks ✗ (not used by HotSpot)

  ── Core algorithm ──
  MARK   : traverse object graph from GC roots, mark live
  SWEEP  : reclaim unmarked objects
  COMPACT: slide survivors together (avoid fragmentation)
  COPY   : move survivors to new space (young gen)

  ── Collector trade-offs ──
  Serial    : 1 thread, tiny heaps
  Parallel  : many threads, max throughput (batch)
  G1        : region-based, pause-time goal (default)
  ZGC/Shen. : mostly concurrent, sub-ms pause, huge heaps

  Contract: app NEVER frees heap manually; drop references →
            object becomes unreachable → collector reclaims it.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Garbage collection is the JVM's automatic memory management, and the core idea is reachability. The collector starts from a set of garbage-collection roots, which are things that are definitely alive, like local variables on the stacks of running threads, static fields, and active thread objects, and it follows every reference from those roots, marking each object it can reach as live. Anything it cannot reach is garbage. The big advantage of reachability over simple reference counting is that it correctly collects cycles, where two objects reference each other but nothing from a root reaches either of them.

The classic algorithm is mark-and-sweep. In the mark phase it walks the object graph from the roots and marks the live objects, and in the sweep phase it reclaims everything that was not marked. Plain sweeping leaves fragmentation, so collectors add a compaction phase that slides live objects together, or they use copying, which moves the survivors into a fresh space and abandons the old one wholesale. Copying is naturally fragmentation-free, which is exactly why the young generation uses it.

This sits on top of a generational heap, because most objects die young. New objects are allocated in the young generation and reclaimed by frequent, cheap minor collections, while objects that keep surviving are promoted to the old generation, which is collected rarely by more expensive major or full collections. On top of all this, the JVM gives me a choice of collectors that trade throughput against pause time: Serial for tiny heaps, Parallel for maximum throughput, G1 as the modern region-based default that targets a pause-time goal by collecting the most garbage-heavy regions first, and ZGC or Shenandoah for very large heaps that need sub-millisecond pauses by doing most work concurrently.

In my banking work the practical consequence is that I never free memory by hand; I just make sure that once a temporary object like a per-request receipt is no longer referenced, nothing from a root reaches it, and the collector reclaims it automatically, cycles included. I also choose the collector to fit the workload, so a latency-sensitive payment API uses G1 or ZGC for small predictable pauses, while a nightly statement batch uses Parallel for raw throughput because longer pauses are acceptable. One senior nuance I always add is that stop-the-world pauses exist because the collector needs a consistent view of the object graph, so picking a collector is really choosing how much pause I can tolerate against how much throughput I need. So my complete answer is that garbage collection reclaims unreachable objects by marking from roots and sweeping the rest, optionally compacting or copying to avoid fragmentation, runs on a generational heap for efficiency, and offers several collectors so I can tune the throughput-versus-pause trade-off for each service.
